source.title: Scaling Laws for Masked-Reconstruction Transformers on Single-Cell Transcriptomics

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and symbols have minor formatting or extraction artifacts, but the reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests parameter- and data-size scaling in a new modality and training regime: masked-reconstruction transformers on single-cell RNA-seq data.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own parameter-scaling results and a fixed-step data-size sweep. Prior language-model scaling results are cited background, not rows. The residual-heterogeneity diagnostic and NLL calibration reruns concern loss interpretation rather than a listed claim version; downstream evaluations are discussed as future work, not reported.
record.test_reason: The study fits L = aP^−α + c to its own masked-reconstruction loss across six model sizes (533 to 1.0×10^8 parameters) on single-cell RNA-seq. This is a new modality and objective, so it bears on V5. It does not test language-model loss, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, shape or downstream tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that validation MSE follows a power law in parameters with an identifiable floor in the standardized V = 512, D = 200k setup, and that test MSE follows the same pattern. Returns diminish beyond about 20M parameters. The fixed-step data-size sweep does not yield a clean L(D) law. The floor corresponds to about 2.3 bits per masked gene, but only under an approximate homoscedastic Gaussian assumption.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses masked reconstruction of continuous single-cell gene expression and MSE, rather than language-model cross-entropy. It varies parameter count in one standardized setting and does not conduct a compute-optimal allocation experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The data-size result depends on holding training steps fixed while dataset size varies, which changes effective epochs; the authors state this prevents a clean data-size estimate. The parameter sweep holds the dataset and optimization hyperparameters fixed.
record.problems: The authors note a limited useful model-size range, no matched full data/vocabulary/compute matrix, a fixed-step data-size sweep that is not definitive, and use of MSE rather than a natively trained likelihood objective. The full six-size Gaussian NLL results are derived from MSE; direct NLL reruns cover only XXS and TINY. The reported residual heterogeneity also makes the homoscedastic entropy conversion approximate.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the direct-NLL calibration reruns or residual-heterogeneity diagnostic: they assess the MSE-to-entropy interpretation, not a listed scaling-law version. The data-size sweep’s individual plotted points are not separately tabulated in the text; its reported aggregate fit and interpretation are recorded in data-size-fit.

untested.parts: A clean data-size law (the sweep is confounded by fixed steps). Compute scaling L(C). Other tissues, species or modalities. Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. A natively trained likelihood objective (only XXS/TINY direct-NLL reruns).
Not a language model, and loss is MSE rather than cross-entropy.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger runs.
Shape is co-varied with size and never held at fixed parameter count.
No systematic variation of fitting method, schedule or parameter counting.

missing.what: Power-law fit to Gaussian NLL derived from MSE: α = 0.182, c = 1.592, R² = 0.838, vs α = 0.266 for MSE on the same 18 runs. The exponent depends on the loss metric's transform.
Direct-NLL calibration reruns: XXS 1.768 direct vs 1.790 derived; TINY 1.634 vs 1.654.

record.verdict_notes: Single-author study (also listed with a TMLR venue) using one data subset and one model per size, with shape co-varying with size. The authors call XXS 'too small to be informative', so most of the fitted trend outside XXS spans only about 1.60 to 1.46 MSE. The comparison of exponents with Kaplan and Hoffmann is cross-domain and confounded by metric, so it is not treated as evidence on V7.

versions.untested_parts: The study is not of language models or held-out cross-entropy; it uses masked-reconstruction MSE on single-cell data.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs; the reported parameter fits use the full sweep.
No compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens is measured.
Architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.

Only single-cell RNA-seq masked reconstruction is tested. The study does not test image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning or transfer, and its primary metric is MSE rather than cross-entropy.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The study does not systematically vary fitting choices or estimate compute-optimal splits. The L-size result is described as consistent with the fitted curve, not as a systematic departure from it.

rows.check: State is fine. Note the size of the gap: L (1.477 ± 0.009) is 0.015 worse than M (1.462 ± 0.003), about 1–2 seed SDs. The authors read this as consistent with a curve already near its floor (c ≈ 1.444), not as a reversal.

rows.subject: Standardized sweep, all six model sizes (18 runs)
rows.operation_detail: Fit L(P) = a · P^−α + c to held-out test MSE across the standardized parameter sweep.
rows.measure: Power-law fit to masked reconstruction MSE
rows.note: The authors report that the held-out test fit is nearly identical to the validation fit.

rows.subject: M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated validation MSE across dataset sizes at a fixed 60,000-step budget.
rows.value: β = −0.0023; R² = 0.611; described as nearly flat rather than a clean monotonic decrease
rows.note: The authors caution that fixed steps mean larger datasets are seen for fewer effective epochs, so this is not a definitive dataset-size law.
rows.check: Training steps are held at 60k while D varies, so effective epochs shrink as D grows. Compute is the bottleneck, which the power-law form excludes. The authors say this is 'not yet a definitive L(D) estimate'. A flat fit (β = −0.0023) therefore cannot show presence or absence of data scaling. 'absent' overstates it.

relationships.condition: Standardized V = 512, D = 200k masked-reconstruction sweep, XXS through M, validation and test MSE
relationships.reason: MSE falls monotonically from 2.10 to 1.46 (param-XXS-val … param-M-test). Offset power-law fits give α ≈ 0.27 on both splits with R² ≈ 0.86 (fit-val, fit-test).
relationships.display_finding: MSE decreased monotonically from 2.10 to 1.46, with offset power-law fits giving α≈0.27 and R²≈0.86 on both validation and test splits.

relationships.condition: Upper end of the parameter sweep (about 19M to 100M parameters) at D = 200k, fixed 60k steps
relationships.reason: L is slightly worse than M on both splits (param-L-val, param-L-test vs param-M-val, param-M-test). Gains stop within about one order of magnitude of the top of the range, and the fit's R² is only about 0.86 (fit-val).
relationships.display_finding: The largest model performed slightly worse than the medium model on validation and test splits, while the overall fit achieved R² of about 0.86.
